Marco Rubio, the secretary of state denied on Monday that the United ⁠States had paused some intelligence sharing with Ukraine, contradicting Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Rubio, speaking to reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan on Monday morning, said ⁠intelligence was in fact never interrupted in the first place.

double quotation mark“I don’t know where ​he’s getting these things ‌or why he’s saying these ‌things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There’s ‌been no pause.

double quotation mark“What he should be focused on, and what we want to be focused on, is bringing an end to this war. That’s what he should be focused on.”

Volodymyr Zelenskyy had thanked the Trump administration on Sunday for resuming intelligence sharing between the two countries, but maintained the US had intentionally throttled its Starlink satellite internet access so that Donald Trump could send a “message” in his ongoing feud with the Ukrainian president.

In an interview on NBC, Zelenskyy said the US had “unblocked” intelligence on impending Russian ballistic missile strikes, which have pounded the country’s energy infrastructure as winter draws in.

“It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by the American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works,” Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press. “Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. And we didn’t get it during ballistic attacks during three days.”

Zelenskyy also said that Elon Musk’s SpaceX was responsible for suddenly limiting the speed at which Starlink terminals worked in Ukraine, hampering drone operations on the frontlines as well as some air defence missions.

“It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed,” he said. “And technically, SpaceX did it.”

Vice-president JD Vance expected to hold rally in North Carolina

The US vice-president JD Vance is expected to hold rally in North Carolina on Monday as the Trump administration continues ramping up rallies to support candidates in the 2026 midterm elections.

Vance’s visit comes as Republicans look to gain ground in North Carolina’s Senate race, as well as in two key US House races. Republican Michael Whatley, whom Trump endorsed, is running against former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper for the seat vacated by Republican US Senator Thom Tillis, who is not seeking reelection.

Henderson, in the heart of the state’s 11th congressional district, and Greenville, just outside the 1st congressional district are where voters strongly supported Trump in 2024 but now, as voters face rising gas and grocery prices, are in play. Democratic victories there could help them flip control of Congress.

Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence in order to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow.

Yuri Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, said on television on Monday morning that Ukraine had not received a warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv at around 11pm. Earlier, a Ukrainian government official had told the Guardian the US had not warned the capital about the impending missile strike.

Ukraine did receive a warning before a successive strike, at 3am, Ihnat added.

“Once again, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack in multiple waves throughout the night, and once again, there was no warning from our partners,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post on Monday morning.

“When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners,” the president added.

Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump will attend a campaign rally in Kansas later today, where incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall is in an unexpectedly close race with Democrat Adam Hamilton.

Marshall’s medical billing scandal is threatening to erode his support, though he is still favored to win.

Hamilton, the founder of the largest Methodist congregation in the US, won in a crowded Democratic primary earlier this year.

Hamilton won 35% of the vote in the 11-candidate Democratic primary. His campaign announced he had broken a quarterly fundraising record in the state, and two major election forecasters say the Senate race has grown more competitive since Hamilton won his party’s primary.

Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and more than half a century has passed since one of their nominees even came close.

Donald Trump posted on Truth Social on Sunday that “restoration work will begin” next month to a historic public golf course in Washington DC despite a federal judge’s court order to pause his plans over environmental and historic preservation concerns. He wrote that the facility would be transformed into “one of the Best and Most Spectacular Golf Courses anywhere in the World”.

Ilhan Omar’s attorneys have asked the US Department of Justice to return property that federal agents removed days earlier from her home during a search. The lawyers for the Minnesota Democrat contended that the seizure as “neither justified nor lawful”, according to a letter published on Friday. The federal investigation into Omar was launched just weeks ahead of the 3 November midterms, in which Omar is on the ballot.

Former US president Barack Obama condemned comments by Trump’s “border czar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip Omar of her citizenship and deport her. Obama wrote Sunday morning, on X, that “the full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.

title: French PM blames ‘ultra-left’ for exploiting protests as he seeks partial curfews – Europe live
excerpt:
Sébastien Lecornu says new measures will be put in place from tonight

Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after 2,400 arrests across France

French PM Lecornu says he has asked prefects to impleme...
body_text:
Sébastien Lecornu says new measures will be put in place from tonight

Macron criticises ‘unbridled violence’ after 2,400 arrests across France

French PM Lecornu says he has asked prefects to implement “a number of partial curfews” in certain “localised” urban areas to stop further disorder, which he attributes to “the extreme-left” and some criminal elements.

We will no doubt hear more on this from local authorities, as in the example of Marseille (10:32).

He also says the government is determined to respond to the events as needed, and if declaring a state of emergency is deemed necessary, they would do so – but that’s a major decision to make and currently not being considered.

He says be believes “there is an agenda of chaos being pushed by the far-left,” with the intention of disrupting next year’s presidential election, and that’s why he urges the NR leaders to attend his briefing later today, despite their plans no to do so (12:20).

Lecornu also says that there will be a “strong” response from the country’s judiciary, cracking down on the violence and crime on the margins of the protests. Investigators are also looking through social media footage, where rioters often did not wear masks.

New measures to stop riots from reoccurring will be put in place starting tonight, but tomorrow’s football game between PSG and Barcelona is currently scheduled to still go ahead.

He also says that furlough measures for businesses affected by riots will kick in on Tuesday to ensure all jobs are saved despite any disruption to business operations in the build up to the busy Christmas period.

He says there will also be further targeted measures, but with little detail at this stage.

Separately, the government will also push to expedite various assessments required to pay out any insurance claims.

Lecornu also says that the right to legitimate protest needs to be safeguarded and considered separately from the riots and clashes with police forces.

German police have said that two men turned themselves in after a security fence was damaged at the airport in the city of Leipzig. The incident had sparked fears as it took place at the same airport where an attack with an explosives-laden drone happened in August, an incident German authorities attributed to Russia.

Authorities had been investigating how a gaping hole was cut into a fence around the airport. The two men say they lost control of the car and crashed through the fence, then left the scene of the accident and arranged for the car to be towed away. AP reports that German police say the car has been seized and the investigation is continuing.

As promised, we have an update from Sweden, with the Centre party’s Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist given a chance to lead talks about the new government in the country.

Thand Ringqvist welcomed the opportunity to lead the discussions and said she would look to progress the talks, but made it clear she had no intention of becoming the next prime minister.

She will try to break a deadlock among the four opposition parties that emerged with a theoretical majority in the new parliament after last month’s elections, but continue to disagree on the composition of the future government.

The Centre party has ruled out being in government with the Left, while the Left has demanded a place in government in return for its cooperation. Without an agreement, the opposition bloc would not have a majority in the new parliament.

Thand Ringqvist will have to report back on the progress of her talks by the end of the week.

The move by the parliament’s speaker Andreas Norlén comes days after the Social Democrats leader and the September election winner Magdalena Andersson failed in her efforts to unite the opposition in the first attempt.

Outgoing prime minister Ulf Kristersson told Swedish broadcaster SVT it was the “logical” decision to give the theoretical opposition bloc another go at forming the next administration.

The European Commission has condemned “unacceptable” acts of “arson, looting and attacks on people or public buildings” in France over the weekend, but stressed the right to peaceful protests was “a fundamental right … and must be protected.”

EU internal affairs spokesperson Markus Lammert said:

“The right to peaceful protest is a fundamental right in all democratic countries and must be protected. Those who demonstrate peacefully must not be conflated with those who commit violence. Arson, looting and attacks on people or public buildings are unacceptable.

We support the efforts of the French authorities to protect people, property and public institutions in full respect of fundamental rights.

It is national authorities that are competent for law enforcement matters, and investigations are currently ongoing at national level.”

He says there will also be further targeted measures, but with little detail at this stage.

Separately, the government will also push to expedite various assessments required to pay out any insurance claims.

Lecornu also says that the right to legitimate protest needs to be safeguarded and considered separately from the riots and clashes with police forces.

We are expecting to hear from France’s prime minister Sébastien Lecornu later today, but he is currently chairing an emergency meeting on the events of the weekend.

Party leaders will also meet with the PM to discuss the political fallout from the protests.

Curiously, the far-right National Rally party will not be represented neither by its presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, nor its prime ministerial candidate, Jordan Bardella, but a more junior figure, media reported.

In the meantime, Paris prosecutor said at least 145 people were still in custody following “various acts of vandalism, looting and attacks on law enforcement,” as reported by Le Figaro.

Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni will hold a crisis meeting with top security officials on Monday after two days of ransacking and looting in Milan allegedly perpetrated by gangs of hooded youths.

The unrest began on Saturday on the fringes of a protest against the rising cost of living. There were also clashes between police and protesters in Turin and Bologna.

In Milan, more than 200 were detained by police, allegedly responsible for ransacking shops and smashing windows, including in the area surrounding the city’s Duomo. According to reports in the Italian press on Monday, 80% were minors, with many responding to appointments made on social media and sharing selfies as they bragged about the damage caused.

They were not believed to have been affiliated with any political party or organised groups or movements.

Meloni said on Saturday that the perpetrators were “thugs who exploit demonstrations to spread chaos, attack those who guarantee security, and hold entire cities to hostage”.

“To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not,” she wrote on X.

During her more than four years in power, Meloni has enacted tough security measures, including against peaceful protesters.

In July, her cabinet approved so-called “anti-maranza” legislation in response to a rise in child gangs and youth delinquency in city centres. “Maranza” is a slang term used to describe gangs of delinquent youths, usually coming from suburban areas.

Opposition politicians often accuse the government of using security as a propaganda tool, arguing that Italy’s leaders do little to address core issues such as education, housing and living conditions in marginalised areas.

There are no signs of French protests stopping anytime soon: the yellow vest movement, de gilets jaunes, has just announced a “second act” of protests for upcoming Saturday, 24 October – and then again a week after that, too.

The idea is to “keep the momentum going” until another major demonstration planned for 5 November, a group member told AFP.

Protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre museum in Paris in support of a nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”, the museum’s management and unions told AFP.

The museum could not open as scheduled because of a protest led by students from the Ecole du Louvre, management said. A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”

Back to France, the authorities in Marseille have just issued a ban of any public gatherings and demonstrations “throughout the entire commune” from midday to 8pm.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has responded to the latest wave of Russian attacks on Ukraine, confirming Ukraine had no prior warning from the US and seemingly accusing Washington of being in the state of denial about the reality of the war.

“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” he said.

“They again targeted energy facilities and infrastructure, but a medical clinic, a school, a metro station, and ordinary residential buildings were also damaged.”

Showing growing frustration with the attacks and continued criticism from US president Donald Trump, he said:

“Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end. We have responded positively to EVERY ceasefire proposal. Russia’s response, time and again, has been ballistic missiles, “shaheds,” and killings.

Putin not only doesn’t want to end this war – he doesn’t even want to take any steps toward de-escalation. EVERY ONE of our partners has experienced this firsthand when they heard Russia’s refusals.

And it is crucial to call things what they are. To call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine defend lives. When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine’s air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners.

The reality is that the war continues, and it continues solely because of Russian strikes and Russia’s desire to drag this war out.”

Italian police also clashed with protesters who threw stones and looted shops in Milan on Sunday during demonstrations over the rising cost of living, as lorry drivers blocked roads across southern Italy in protest at soaring fuel prices linked to the war in Iran.

Footage showed police in riot gear firing teargas and using water cannon after several hundred hooded protesters smashed shop windows and set bins alight in the area around Piazza del Duomo in central Milan.

The clashes echoed scenes of violence in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.

Meanwhile, lorry drivers have caused widespread disruption across southern Italy, blocking major roads and creating huge traffic jams in Sicily, Puglia and Calabria in protest at the mounting financial pressure on the haulage industry.

Hundreds of petrol stations have run out of fuel, while supermarkets are beginning to report shortages of several products, particularly fresh food. Pharmacies have also been affected, raising concerns about disruption to essential supplies.

“We are asking the government to urgently convene a meeting with industry associations. Otherwise, we will consider a nationwide strike,” said Pasquale Russo, president of Conftrasporto, an association representing Italian haulage companies.

“The situation is very concerning because the excessive price increases affecting the haulage industry have created a highly tense situation among transport companies, leading to spontaneous protests in some areas of the country,” he added.

In several parts of southern Italy, petrol stations have run out of both petrol and diesel, with motorists facing long queues at the few filling stations still operating. The road blockades have also caused extensive traffic disruption, with fears growing that prolonged protests could further disrupt supplies of food, fuel and other essential goods.

French president Emmanuel Macron has declined interior minister Laurent Nuñez’s offer to resign after widespread riots over the weekend, despite “failures in anticipation and intelligence” that were deemed to worsen the crisis engulfing the country.

Macron said Nuñez should stay to ‌ensure a chain of command is retained within the police and security forces, and has also asked Nuñez to set up ‌as quickly as possible new approaches to deal with looters, ​the Élysée Palace added, quoted by Reuters.

Macron has asked the minister to “put in place new operational methods for security forces” to get a grip over the crisis.

Saturday, one of the most violent days of unrest in years, left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country.

In a TV interview on Monday, Nuñez admitted that the police “lost control” in some cities during the protests.

In an address to the nation last night, Macron criticised “unbridled violence”.

“Watching these images, we have all asked ourselves how could French people do this to France?” he said.

I will bring you more updates on this today.

Separately, I will also be keeping an eye on Ukraine, after another night of heavy attacks by Russia killing at least one and injuring eight people, and with conflicting reports about whether Kyiv authorities had been warned about the strikes.

We should also get an update from Sweden, as the parliament’s speaker is set to decide on the next step in the government formation process there.

I will bring you all the key updates here.

It’s Monday, 19 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

title: Personal attacks fire up debate before Brazil's run-off vote
excerpt:
Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva are competing for the presidency in a run-off election due on Sunday

Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, ...
body_text:
Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva are competing for the presidency in a run-off election due on Sunday

Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election.

Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was  hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters.

But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further.

In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula.

Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open.

Flávio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election.

The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.

Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time".

Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks.

Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments.

"The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression."

Lucas Aragão from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin".

Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da Tendências Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off.

Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking.

One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk.

Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia".

Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen."

He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt).

Bolsonaro had highlighted the initials for the Workers' Party on his hand

"Take a piece of paper and a pen and jot down 'corrupt' and you'll see that it has two letters in the middle here together," he said, pointing to PT, the initials of the Workers' Party in Portuguese.

Bolsonaro, who is campaigning on a iron-fist approach to crime, challenged Lula to explain why crime rates had gone up during his four years in power.

He also alleged, without providing any evidence, that "the majority of convicts vote for Lula".

Lula shot back with a thinly veiled reference to Flávio's convicted father, Jair, saying; "I wish it was 100%, even your father".

Brazil sees record fall in Amazon deforestation as key election looms

Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula

Right-wing Flávio Bolsonaro wins first round of Brazil election

title: On Iran, Israel’s opposition is even more hawkish than Netanyahu
excerpt:
When Israel launched a sweeping military assault on Iran with the United States in February, the Israeli government enjoyed overwhelming support from the Jewish Israeli public.

Opposition parties len...
body_text:
When Israel launched a sweeping military assault on Iran with the United States in February, the Israeli government enjoyed overwhelming support from the Jewish Israeli public.

Opposition parties lent their support to the army and backed the audacious step. Enmity towards the government in Iran is an issue mainstream Zionist parties agree on.

Then in June, Israel’s role in the confrontation halted abruptly with an announcement from US President Donald Trump, who said Iran and Israel had agreed to stop attacking each other.

That announcement – and Netanyahu’s decision to abide by it at the time – were unpopular in Israel. According to the Israel Democracy Institute, 65 to 70 percent of Jewish Israelis believe that stopping the war did not serve Israel’s national security interests.

As Israelis prepare to vote in national elections on October 27, Iran remains an important election issue for many. Opposition parties present Iran as an example of what they say are Netanyahu’s many failures. They promise to reset security and foreign policy if they’re elected.

The frontrunner, Gadi Eisenkot, says the conflict is unfinished. While saying that a change in Iran’s government was an unrealistic goal, Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of doing little to dismantle Iran’s nuclear programme. In September at the inauguration of his new party, Yashar, Eisenkot told supporters: “Ultimately, it must end in the destruction or dismantling of the Iranian nuclear programme, a goal not yet achieved with 440kg [970lb] of highly enriched uranium already there, which could quickly be turned into several nuclear devices.”

Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, who is now the head of the opposition in the Knesset, accuses Netanyahu of a strategic failure. He recently told the Atlantic Council that toppling the administration in Tehran is a realistic objective that requires a military escalation: “What Israel should do or the alliance should do is bomb all the energy facilities, especially on Kharg Island, but other places as well in order to make sure that the Iranian economy is demolished. And the reason is that it’s the only thing that will overturn the regime.”

Bombing this civilian infrastructure was actually something Netanyahu had lobbied for himself. An international outcry about such bombings likely constituting war crimes and Trump’s refusal to offer backing put the brakes on the plan.

Naftali Bennett, another former prime minister, says Israel must ensure its military dominance over the entire region. For Bennett, toppling the government in Iran and crushing it is a must. But he says that is not enough. The right-wing politician calls Qatar an “enemy” and says Turkiye is “the new Iran”, going as far as saying that military confrontation with the NATO member was inevitable.

“We will build an alliance of moderate forces in the region against the Islamist forces, against Iran, against Qatar, Turkiye and all the radical forces. We will take proactive actions to shape the region,” Bennett recently told supporters.

Eisenkot and other opposition leaders do not rule out renewed confrontations. They focus on their confidence in the military and security establishment in assessing the dangers and dealing with them appropriately.

But opposition leaders have voiced concern that Netanyahu might resort to military escalation before the elections to tilt the balance in his favour or even disrupt them altogether – even though the prime minister said last week that he did not plan to attack Iran before the vote.

Those fears were elevated after Netanyahu posted a video from the Tel Nof Airbase warning that Israel’s enemies might attack before the elections. Other news reports said Netanyahu has shared intelligence on new threats from Iran with the US president.

Netanyahu was quickly rebuked by opposition leaders, who accused him of “political fearmongering”.

Lapid openly questioned Netanyahu’s motives. Lapid also accused him of using the Israeli military and bases as “backdrops” for election campaign videos.

Ultimately, most Israeli opposition parties and leaders aren’t opposed to war with Iran, and many are in fact even more hawkish in their approach towards Tehran than Netanyahu. They just don’t want a new military escalation before the elections.

title: Italian PM Meloni to hold emergency meeting after weekend of violent clashes
excerpt:
More than 200 people were arrested across the weekend, according to Italian media

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is set to hold an emergency security meeting on Monday after protests over the ...
body_text:
More than 200 people were arrested across the weekend, according to Italian media

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is set to hold an emergency security meeting on Monday after protests over the rising cost of living broke out into violent clashes in Milan.

More than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers.

"To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".

Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania.

Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried it was a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".

Speaking to Italian news agency Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".

Clashes began on Saturday and continued into Sunday in Milan. More than 200 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Ansa reported.

The city's prosecutor's office has requested prison sentences for five adults arrested for looting, vandalism and resisting arrest, according to Italian news agency AGI.

Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured.

Violence between protesters and police also rippled into other cities in the north.

Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder.

The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting.

"Do not be ambiguous about this," she said on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".

Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.

The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.

title: First Thing: US ambassador in rare diplomatic break with Israel over attack on US journalist
excerpt: Mike Huckabee condemns attack on Washington Post photojournalist that has drawn lukewarm response from Israeli authorities. Plus, Japan is attempting to boldly go where no space mission has gone befor...
body_text:
Mike Huckabee condemns attack on Washington Post photojournalist that has drawn lukewarm response from Israeli authorities. Plus, Japan is attempting to boldly go where no space mission has gone before

Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here

Good morning. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, has denounced a settler attack that left the Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine badly beaten and needing surgery as a “despicable act of terror”.

Levine, 63, an award-winning journalist who lives in Israel, was set upon last Friday by masked Israeli settlers who used clubs and other weapons to attack Palestinians attempting to harvest their olives. The photographer, who is in hospital recovering from hand surgery, broken ribs and other injuries, said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes.

Huckabee said: “We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this. Attacking a female photographer is despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards.”

What else has Heidi Levine said about the attack? She said: “I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me. I’ve been covering this region for over 40 years and I have never seen this country in such a state as it is today. I’ve invested decades of blood, sweat and tears into this. They cracked my bones, they haven’t cracked my spirit.”

How have Israeli authorities responded? In a move Levine said left her “shocked and insulted”, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been ambiguous in addressing the assault. He said he condemned “violence against anyone” but referred to the attack as “alleged” and said its circumstances remained unclear.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has criticised “unbridled violence” after one of the most violent days of unrest in years left public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,400 people arrested in cities across the country. Macron said “nothing justifies” violence and that local state officials would be able to ban certain street gatherings if they deemed it necessary. Macron condemned the “failures” he said had led to the crisis, but he refused the resignation of the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez.

What is causing the wave of protests across Europe? School conditions, housing costs and the cost of living have brought demonstrators on to the streets in several countries including Spain, France and Portugal. Protests in Albania against the prime minister, Edi Rama, entered their sixth day on Sunday. Demonstrators there have said they are unhappy with perceived corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.

Ukraine did not receive a warning from the US about an impending Russian missile attack on Sunday evening, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, reviving concerns that Washington is withholding intelligence in order to bully Kyiv into capitulating to Moscow. On Friday, Donald Trump waived a sweeping package of sanctions on Russia. Ukraine has also complained of slowed deliveries of air defence missiles from the US. Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post: “When the supply of missiles for Ukrainian air defence is blocked, and Russia receives sanctions relief or delays, it is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners.”

Barack Obama has condemned comments by Donald Trump’s “border tsar” that the Republican presidential administration could “of course” strip the Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar of her citizenship and deport her. Obama wrote: “The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president.” He urged all Americans to defend Omar, regardless of their political beliefs.

The captain of a flydubai flight who was attacked by a co-pilot who intended to crash the plane has described ⁠blocking axe blows to his head and screaming for help as he reached to open the cockpit door.

Capt Smit ⁠Machchhar has been hailed ⁠as a ​hero for his role in averting disaster on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month, helping to thwart what the UAE ⁠attorney general has said was an attempted suicide attack by the co-pilot who intended to crash the plane into Ben Gurion airport.

A Kansas driver who allegedly killed two people and hurt 10 others at a soccer game has been released from custody. According to authorities, the woman has been released without charges, pending further investigation.

The Australian MP Helen Haines is in critical condition after a suspected attack outside her office. Reports suggest she was deliberately targeted with a vehicle.

A CBS reporter has apologized and deleted a post praising someone who heckled Abdul El-Sayed. The Democratic Michigan US Senate candidate had been asked: “Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?”

The Roman Catholic church has upheld the excommunication of a Louisiana deacon who resigned from the clergy after a priest molested his son.

Amelia Earhart researchers have left a remote atoll empty-handed after suspected “plane debris” was found to be a clump of trees.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s buzzy film was shown on only 855 screens and had the biggest documentary opening in North America since Fahrenheit 9/11 in 2004.

Lex McMenamin reports on how the pro-LGBTQ+ sports fanbase is pushing a message of inclusion in the face of anti-trans attacks.

Influencers using beauty spots, tourist attractions and high-end destinations to stage photoshoots has led to some places introducing restricted hours for filming and even outright bans as part of a backlash against “content creators”. Of course, you could follow Georgina McNamara’s lead and just delete Instagram completely to rediscover the joys of a truly private life.

Lois Beckett has been in San Clemente where rapid coastal erosion threatens coastal homes and economies, and a town is reckoning with the reality of climate crisis.

This month’s biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia, aims to push governments to meet the 23 targets agreed at Cop15 in 2022. Patrick Greenfield explains what you need to know.

Japan is to launch a spacecraft on the world’s first mission to bring back samples from Phobos. Scientists hope the mission, which is expected to take five years, will provide clues to how Phobos and its smaller sibling Deimos formed, and hopefully even shed light on the origins of life in the solar system.

title: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
excerpt:
The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and preparations for a stock market listing

Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI develop...
body_text:
The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and preparations for a stock market listing

Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing.

The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline.

The fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said.

The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours.

“AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost.

It said that while it had already committed $200m to addressing the issue, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”

The company, which is preparing to list on the stock market, has called for a slowdown in breakneck development of AI, a warning later echoed by rivals such as OpenAI.

Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round. The company is reportedly considering a $1.5tn valuation when it floats on the stock market, with an IPO planned for November.

Last week, Anthropic said some of its AI models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners.

It said that once this happens, the models would be able to power themselves without the need of datacentres.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and founder of SpaceX, responded to Anthropic’s plans for a public benefit fund on social media by pledging to give some of his own shares away.

“I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” he wrote. “This is what I will be doing.”

He later announced: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.”

Shares in SpaceX, which is listed on the Nasdaq in the US, rose by 1% in pre-market trading on Monday. The company has lost about 9% of its value since it joined the stock market in June.

OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, also reportedly engaged in early talks to give a 5% stake in its organisation to the US government.

Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, was established as a public benefit corporation. It means that all of the company’s directors must balance financial returns with its public interest mission.

title: ‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after independent MP Helen Haines critically injured
excerpt:
Anthony Albanese says his thoughts are with Indi MP after arrest of driver in Wangaratta

Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria?

Get our new political email, free app or daily ne...
body_text:
Anthony Albanese says his thoughts are with Indi MP after arrest of driver in Wangaratta

Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria?

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The independent MP Helen Haines has been critically injured in an alleged attack involving a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, confirmed on Monday night that a man was in custody after the alleged attack on Haines that was now being investigated by the Australian federal police (AFP), Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce.

He said the motive for the alleged attack was not known, and would not comment on whether the suspect was known to police.

“Helen Haines is incredibly hard-working. She is fiercely intelligent, but most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across the parliament, and from everyone who comes into contact with her, she is a well-loved member of her community, and this will come as an incredible shock to that community,” Albanese said.

He said he respected her integrity most of all.

“It doesn’t mean we always agree, but I always agree that her motives are good,” Albanese said.

“Our thoughts remain with Helen Haines at this very difficult time.”

The prime minister and Victoria police said they were not aware of any recent direct threats to Haines.

Albanese later said on the ABC’s 7.30 program that while he did not want to speculate on the motivation for the alleged attack, he had repeatedly warned “the temperature has increased in recent times” in relation to politics.

He had feared that would increase the risk of political violence occurring in Australia that had been seen in other western democracies.

Albanese, who became emotional at times during the interview, said he first was told that Haines had been injured in a car accident, before being informed it was allegedly a deliberate act.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also said there had been an increase in threats towards politicians.

“The year before last, we had 951 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against various high officeholders,” he said.

“The more recent financial year, that 951 has gone to 1,067.”

In a statement, Haines’s family confirmed that she had been injured and thanked bystanders for their assistance.

“This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care,” they said in the statement.

“We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response.

“Our family, and Helen’s staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media.

Haines was airlifted to hospital in Melbourne.

In a statement, Victoria police said a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, about 10km from Wangaratta, was in custody and that a knife had allegedly been found in his car. They alleged he had been detained by a passerby when he exited the car.

The statement said the woman that was struck was in a critical condition.

“Police have arrested a man after a woman was struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta this afternoon.

“It is understood a white Toyota LandCruiser struck the 65-year-old woman outside an office on Murphy Street about 3.35pm.”

Police said that they were investigating as to whether it was an intentional act, and it was not known if “the parties are known to each other”.

Speaking at the scene, acting Supt Ashley Mason said it was being treated as an isolated incident.

He said that the bystanders who assisted in the arrest and with Haines should be commended for acting as they did when confronted with a “horrific tragic incident”.

It was a “dynamic incident” with an extensive crime scene, he said.

The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, said he knew the alleged attack would be devastating for the Wangaratta community and all those Haines represented.

“I am deeply appalled by this [alleged] violent attack on Helen Haines,” he said in a statement.

“My thoughts – and the thoughts of all Victorians – are with Helen, her family, her friends, her colleagues and her community.”

The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said the incident was a “shocking day for our nation”, and that political attacks cannot be normalised in Australia.

The Liberal leader said he was “deeply saddened and distressed” and was praying for Haines and her family.

“This is a shocking day for our nation … Australians will be angry and appalled by the [alleged] attack on Helen outside her electorate office in Wangaratta,” he said in a statement on social media.

In a social media post, theNationals MP Michael McCormack said it was “such awful news”.

“Sending my love and best wishes to Helen Haines for a full and speedy recovery,” McCormack said.

Police were expected to release a statement regarding the incident on Monday night.

Haines has represented the electorate of Indi since 2019.

Asio has in recent years repeatedly warned about the rising threat of politically motivated violence.

“Political differences, political debates and political protests are essential parts of a healthy democracy,” Mike Burgess, the Asio director general, said in 2025.

“Unfortunately, here and overseas, levels of personal grievance and frustration are growing.

“Rightly or wrongly some Australians feel dispossessed, disaffected, disenfranchised … many of the aggrieved do not necessarily espouse violent views, but may still see violence as a legitimate way to effect political or societal change.”

He added last year that although Australia’s terrorism threat level remained at probable, the system was not “designed for a situation like the one we now face”.

“We do know the environment is degrading and acts of politically motivated violence are becoming more likely than probable suggests,” he said.

“Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack.”

title: WNBA silent after Finals teams skip national anthem despite rule requiring players to stand and line up
excerpt:
The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries left the floor moments before the national anthem during WNBA Finals Game 1, then returned seconds after it ended.

SAN FRANCISCO – The WNBA’s own rulebook...
body_text:
The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries left the floor moments before the national anthem during WNBA Finals Game 1, then returned seconds after it ended.

SAN FRANCISCO – The WNBA’s own rulebook calls for players, coaches and trainers to stand and line up along the sidelines or foul line during the national anthem. Both of its Finals teams left the court for Saturday’s performance, and the league has not answered OutKick’s questions about their absences.

And with Game 2 set for Monday night, neither team has told OutKick whether it plans to be on the floor for the anthem this time.

GABBY WILLIAMS DELIVERS LATE AS VALKYRIES SHUT DOWN ANGEL REESE, DREAM TO WIN WNBA FINALS OPENER

Neither the Atlanta Dream nor the Golden State Valkyries were on the court during the national anthem prior to Game 1 of the 2026 WNBA Finals. (NBAE via Getty Images)

Both teams were warming up on the court Saturday at Chase Center before leaving just ahead of the national anthem. Within seconds of the performance ending, the players were jogging back onto the floor.

Getting an explanation for why the teams chose to be off the floor for those roughly two minutes has been incredibly difficult.

OutKick contacted the WNBA, and both the Dream and Valkyries on Saturday, then followed up with all three Sunday.

None answered the anthem questions before publication.

OutKick also attended all five of Saturday’s pregame and postgame press conferences but was not called on. We had planned to ask about the teams’ plans before the game and their absence from the anthem afterward.

The follow-up questions to both teams were straightforward: Why were their players off the court during the Game 1 anthem? Would they be there for Game 2? Had the WNBA communicated any instructions or expectations about the anthem since Saturday?

ANGEL REESE'S WNBA FINALS APPEARANCE AFTER CHICAGO EXIT RAISES QUESTIONS ABOUT WINNING MENTALITY

Angel Reese and her Atlanta Dream teammates were not on the floor during the national anthem prior to Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. (Getty Images)

The WNBA’s 2026 official rulebook includes an anthem provision covering players, coaches and trainers. It calls for them to form a standing line at a sideline or foul line while the anthem plays.

The league has not answered OutKick’s questions about its anthem requirements, whether any discipline is planned or under consideration, or whether it will instruct either team to be present for Game 2.

We also asked the league to confirm whether both teams would be on the court for Monday's anthem.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

If Saturday's absences were simply part of the teams' pregame routines, both have had an opportunity to explain that. Neither has done so in response to OutKick’s inquiries.

But a pregame routine that keeps players off the floor during the national anthem deserves scrutiny.

HOSTILE VALKYRIES FANS VERBALLY ATTACKED WOMEN'S SPORTS ACTIVISTS AT WNBA FINALS GAME 1 IN SAN FRANCISCO

The Chase Center interior is shown during Game 1 of the WNBA Finals between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries on Oct. 17, 2026, in San Francisco, Calif. (NBAE via Getty Images)

title: Beau Lamarre-Condon told officer friend ‘I love you’ and ‘not everything in the news is true’ after arrest, court told
excerpt:
Accused asked fellow police officer how law enforcement would respond to reports of gunshots days before alleged murders, court hears

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau...
body_text:
Accused asked fellow police officer how law enforcement would respond to reports of gunshots days before alleged murders, court hears

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Beau Lamarre-Condon allegedly told a friend “I love you’” and “not everything in the news is true” a month after he was arrested over a double murder, a court has heard.

Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

Dayna Schagen, who was a friend of Lamarre-Condon and is an officer with the NSW police, told his trial on Monday about a call she received in late March 2024, about a month after the alleged murders.

She initially did not pick up because it came at about 9pm from a number she did not recognise and she believed it was “rude to call after dinner time on a weeknight”.

But after the number dialled a second time, she picked up the phone and immediately recognised Lamarre-Condon’s voice.

According to her police statement, which was read to the court, he said, “Dayna, it’s Beau,” and she responded, “what the fuck, why are you calling me”.

He then said: “I just wanted to tell you that I love you and before you do anything, you need to know not everything in the news is true. It will all come out in court.”

The court heard Schagen then cut off Lamarre-Condon and said: “You killed two people, why would I ever want to speak to you again?”

She then told her boss about the phone call and made a statement to police about the incident.

Schagen did not have any role in the police investigation into the double murders as an officer.

Earlier on Monday, Schagen told the jury Lamarre-Condon had been seeing Baird on and off during 2023 and had been hoping to turn it into a relationship.

When Baird made it clear he wasn’t interested and the two broke up in April 2023, Lamarre-Condon was “still very much invested in him”, Schagen said.

“I believed that he missed him and still very much wanted to be in a relationship. It was a sore spot for the accused,” she told the court.

Baird ended his involvement with Lamarre-Condon in November 2023.

Lamarre-Condon allegedly told Schagen he had “fucked up” after Baird found out he had gone through Baird’s phone, and blocked a man Baird had been sleeping with, without his knowledge.

When she found out, Schagen told Lamarre-Condon she was “mortified he did something so stupid when they weren’t in a relationship”, the court heard.

“You’ve got no grounds to be pissed off about who he’s sleeping with, you’re not together,” she allegedly told him.

Days before the alleged murders, on 14 February 2024, Lamarre-Condon asked Schagen a “hypothetical question” about work, she told the jury.

He allegedly asked: “If you were at work and there was a job broadcast over the radio for gunshots fired, what would the police response be if someone jumped on the radio and said, ‘we’ve been flagged by a member of the public who said that children were letting fireworks off’?”

She told him police would disregard it and move on due to the sheer volume of jobs she received.

The prosecution clarified to the jury that those with a police radio can hear jobs being broadcast.

After seeing news of Baird and Davies’ disappearance, Schagen sent a message to Lamarre-Condon on 22 February 2024 that said: “Are you ok? Have you spoken to him? What the fuck is going on?”

She did not receive a response, and told the court at this point she believed she had “an indication” Lamarre-Condon was potentially involved.

A day later, she saw he had been active on Facebook’s messaging service and asked him: “Where the fuck are you and what’s all this shit in the media, what’s going on?”

He opened the message but did not respond, the court heard.

She confirmed the conversation they had about police response to reports of gunshots was on her mind and that was why she eventually approached police.

The defence team has claimed Baird and Davies were accidentally shot in two separate struggles with the accused while he acted in “self-defence”.

Lamarre-Condon cleaned up the scene and disposed of the bodies afterwards because he “panicked considerably”, defence lawyer John Stratton SC said.

On Monday afternoon, the jury was shown CCTV footage from 20 February 2024, the day after the alleged murders.

He can be seen buying cleaning equipment from Bunnings Alexandria, withdrawing cash from ATMs across Sydney, eating at Sushi Train Cronulla with a friend, and going back and forth between various locations and Baird’s Paddington home.

The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.
