title: Neto’s brace fires Chelsea past Everton but Martinez head injury mars win
excerpt:
Pedro Neto’s double condemned Everton to a first defeat of the season as Chelsea won 2-0 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium despite the loss of goalkeeper Emi Martinez to a head injury.

Neto opened the sc...
body_text:
Pedro Neto’s double condemned Everton to a first defeat of the season as Chelsea won 2-0 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium despite the loss of goalkeeper Emi Martinez to a head injury.

Neto opened the scoring inside the first minute of the second half on Saturday and secured the three points during the 11 added minutes following the lengthy treatment given to the stricken Martinez.

The Argentinian international was involved in a sickening head clash with Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite and was taken to hospital.

“As far as I know he left the stadium conscious. Right now he’s in the hospital doing the precautionary tests, so let’s see,” said Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso.

A first away win of the season lifts Chelsea above the Toffees into the top four and the Blues also recorded a first clean sheet in 23 Premier League games.

“We needed one of these wins away. We have played very professional, very serious, looking solid. It is a very good win,” added Alonso.

“We need to get many more clean sheets for the rest of the league games but for sure the first one of the season feels good and now we need to keep going this way.”

After a slow start, a fiery-tempered encounter sparked into life when Everton midfielder Harrison Armstrong launched into a tackle on Josh Acheampong for the first of five first-half yellow cards.

That challenge also enlivened the home crowd and spurred Everton on to their best spell of the game.

Thierno Barry was guilty of another wasteful day in front of goal as the Frenchman planted a header from Jack Grealish’s cross too close to Martinez.

Chelsea have made a habit of fast starts under Alonso, but it took until four minutes before half-time to threaten when Moises Caicedo blasted off the bar from a well-worked corner.

Everton were furious that Morgan Rogers escaped a second booking just before the break after a thunderous clash with England teammate James Garner.

That proved to be a huge decision as the visitors this time flew out of the blocks at the start of the second period.

Jorrel Hato got to the byline and his low cross fell to Neto, who had time to control before firing low past Jordan Pickford.

Chelsea had not kept a Premier League clean sheet since January, but were rarely troubled by an Everton side short on forward options, despite the loss of Martinez.

“I just felt that Chelsea had that little bit more flair and ability which we didn’t possess at the right moments today,” said Everton boss David Moyes.

The treatment for Martinez threatened to halt Chelsea’s momentum as they controlled the second half.

Belgian Mike Penders replaced the Chelsea number one for his first Premier League appearance but had little to do bar dealing with a few desperate Everton crosses.

At the other end Pickford made a fine save to deny Joao Pedro.

But Chelsea did get their second goal when Neto coolly stroked into the bottom corner after Jordan Henderson’s free-kick was blocked by the Everton wall.

“We are really ‌‌pleased. Shame for Emi but we wish you all the best. This win is for him,” Neto told TNT Sports after his first Premier League brace.

“We need a clean sheet, to be honest. I think we did a very good game. Emi deserved this, Mike did as well.”

title: Florida fisher dragged into water and killed by 12ft alligator
excerpt:
Steve Hamilton was fishing in Winter Garden when he was attacked by gator, which was later killed

A man fishing at a pond in Florida was killed on Friday by an alligator that was almost 12ft long in ...
body_text:
Steve Hamilton was fishing in Winter Garden when he was attacked by gator, which was later killed

A man fishing at a pond in Florida was killed on Friday by an alligator that was almost 12ft long in a rare kind of animal attack, according to authorities and media reports.

Steve Hamilton, 71, was on the shoreline in the community of Winter Garden when the animal dragged him into the water, the Florida news outlet WOFL reported, citing local police and the state’s fish and wildlife conservation commission.

Emergency crews responded to the park where Hamilton was fishing at about 5.20pm on Friday after receiving a 911 call and attempted to rescue him – but they had difficulty doing so because of nearby alligators, the outlet reported.

Hamilton’s body was recovered from the water a couple of hours later.

Capt Michael Mason of the Winter Garden police department told news media that the alligator had been killed after the fatal attack on Hamilton.

Authorities were not alerted of a gator sighting on Friday at the pond, which is connected to Lake Apopka, Mason said.

The body of water has “tons of alligators in it. That is not uncommon to see alligators in this part of town,” Mason said.

The chief encouraged people to “be aware of your surroundings”.

The gator “looks like it’s docile. It looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous,” Mason said.

Alligator attacks are statistically rare. Nonetheless, at least 34 people have been killed by them in Florida since 1948, according to the Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission, which compiles reports of encounters with the state’s estimated 1.3 million gators.

Hamilton’s death came less than four months after a woman named Brittany Clark was attacked and killed by a 13ft alligator while swimming with her boyfriend in the Econlockhatchee River in Florida’s Seminole county.

Autopsy results released in July showed Clark, 31, struggled for her life before dying from the wounds inflicted on her by the alligator, which was removed from the river and euthanized.

title: Zelenskyy says Trump’s lifting of sanctions on Russia will intensify war in Ukraine
excerpt:
Ukrainian president calls the move a ‘reward’ for Vladimir Putin as Russia strikes country’s power plants

Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable

Volodymyr Z...
body_text:
Ukrainian president calls the move a ‘reward’ for Vladimir Putin as Russia strikes country’s power plants

Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Donald Trump’s decision to roll back sanctions on Russia will intensify the Kremlin’s war in Ukraine, as Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine’s power plants in an attempt to black out the country’s cities before winter.

The Ukrainian president also said he expected the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin.

“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”

In a social media message earlier, Zelenskyy described Trump’s latest actions as a “reward” that would embolden the Russian president.

“A US ⁠sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground,” said Zelenskyy. “We must keep trying to end the ‌war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.”

In its latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia, Trump announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.

The act, named for the late senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the legislation, would have introduced tough new sanctions on Russia including a 100% tariff on major importers of Russian oil such as China and India, as well as sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, financial institutions and shadow fleet of oil tankers.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy said the decision to waive the sanctions would encourage Vladimir Putin to intensify the war in Ukraine and called for support in the US to resurrect the bill.

“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he wrote in a statement. “This law could have – and still can! – help a great deal. But the law needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”

The move was greeted by the Russian presidential envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”

The legislation, which sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps the country’s energy supplies moving, was due to be implemented in two days.

It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.

Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1m tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.

The Trump administration’s decision to waive the sanctions is the latest consequence of a brutal quarrel between Trump and Zelenskyy. Several times this week, the US did not provide intelligence of impending ballistic missile attacks to Ukraine, and the White House reportedly ordered the Pentagon to throttle the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet network used by Ukraine’s armed forces to run its drone operations on the frontline.

“We very much hope – and I personally hope – that the president of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops the strikes on our energy infrastructure, and stops this war,” Zelenskyy said on Saturday. “But once again, you cannot achieve this by restricting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And even less so by lifting sanctions.”

Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he has blamed the war in Ukraine, rather than the closure of the strait of Hormuz, for the worldwide spike in diesel prices. Ukraine unilaterally halted the strikes after Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, but resumed them when it became clear that Russia was stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian power plants and substations.

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had launched one of its worst strikes yet against the country’s energy infrastructure, hitting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities and causing “severe consequences”.

He also indicated that Ukraine’s dwindling stock of anti-air weapons made it difficult to shoot down many of the loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles being launched each night at Ukraine.

“Although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them,” he said, the “sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences.”

title: Hackers hide dangerous fake AI downloads behind Google ads
excerpt: Charles Payne reacts to a new OpenAI report warning about artificial intelligence models cheating and hacking systems. Payne explains the details of the 'hugging face' incident to Bret Baier, arguing ...
body_text:
Charles Payne reacts to a new OpenAI report warning about artificial intelligence models cheating and hacking systems. Payne explains the details of the 'hugging face' incident to Bret Baier, arguing that the AI was not going rogue but simply following its training through a weak backdoor. He breaks down the three categories of artificial intelligence development.

You search Google for Claude, the popular AI assistant, and spot a sponsored result. The link points to Bing, Microsoft's search engine. Nothing immediately screams scam. However, that click could send you through several websites before landing on a convincing fake Claude download page designed to trick you into running a dangerous command on your Mac.

Security researchers at Push Security uncovered a clever attack that uses legitimate search engine links to hide a malicious installer. The technique, which researchers jokingly call "Adception," takes advantage of how Google ads and Bing redirects work. Even more concerning, the fake installer shows one command on the screen while secretly copying another. Here's how the scam works and what you should know before downloading AI software.

Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.

HACKERS HIJACK VERIFIED STREAMING ACCOUNT TO SPREAD MALWARE, RESEARCHERS FIND

Cybersecurity researchers uncovered a fake Claude AI download page that tricks Mac users into running a potentially dangerous Terminal command. (Photo by Phil Barker/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

The attack begins with a Google search for "Claude Mac." According to Push Security, researchers discovered a sponsored search result that displayed bing.com as its destination. That address might seem reassuring because Bing belongs to Microsoft. However, clicking the advertisement sends users through a series of redirects. First, Google's advertising system processes the click. Next, Bing's legitimate click-tracking service forwards the browser to a compromised WordPress website belonging to a South American retailer. Finally, that website sends the visitor to a fake Claude download page.

The final website, claude-desk-code[.]com, imitates the real Claude download experience. It presents what appears to be a legitimate macOS installation option. By the time someone reaches the page, they may have little reason to suspect the journey began with a malicious advertisement. Researchers say the attackers deliberately used a real Bing search result for a compromised website. This allowed the attackers to display Bing's legitimate domain in the Google advertisement while using Bing's click-tracking redirect to send visitors toward the malicious destination.

The scammers added another layer of deception to make their operation harder to detect. The compromised retailer's website checks whether visitors arrived through Bing and whether their browsers send certain information. Meanwhile, the fake Claude website checks whether visitors came from Google or Bing. Someone who visits the malicious website directly may see a 404 error page instead of the fake installer. That behavior can make it harder for security scanners to investigate the attack because they may never encounter the page that victims actually see.

Push Security calls this technique cloaking. Attackers use it to control who reaches their malicious content while showing something harmless to other visitors. In this case, the researchers observed two separate checks designed to protect the attack from unwanted attention. The result is a carefully constructed path that makes a dangerous destination appear more trustworthy than it really is.

Here's where the attack gets particularly sneaky. The fake Claude page displays an installation command that appears to come directly from Anthropic, the company behind Claude. The command references Claude's legitimate website and looks like something a technically confident Mac user might recognize. However, the page's Copy button places a completely different command on the clipboard.

According to Push Security, the substituted command uses Base64 encoding to conceal an attacker-controlled website. When someone runs the pasted command in Mac Terminal, it first displays a reassuring message claiming that Claude is being downloaded from its official website. Behind the scenes, the command decodes the hidden address, downloads a remote script and sends it directly to the Mac's Z shell for execution. That means the person running the command sees references to Claude's legitimate website even though the Mac is executing code from an unrelated server.

This attack follows a technique known as InstallFix, a variation of ClickFix. These scams convince people to execute malicious commands themselves, often by disguising the instructions as a software installation or troubleshooting step. Push Security identified several additional websites associated with the same malicious toolkit, which it tracks internally as AcSig. The researchers found matching installation commands and similar fake installer interfaces across those sites.

The research confirms that the malicious command is designed to download a remote script from an attacker-controlled server and pass it directly to the Mac's Z shell for execution. However, Push Security's published findings do not identify the final payload or establish what the downloaded script does after execution. That uncertainty is important. Running an untrusted Terminal command can give malicious code an opportunity to operate with the permissions of the person executing it. Depending on the script, an attacker could potentially steal information, modify files or install additional software. The researchers have not confirmed those specific outcomes in this campaign.

The bigger concern is how easily the attack can persuade someone to bypass their own caution. The user voluntarily pastes the command, believing it came from a legitimate software provider. Meanwhile, the actual destination stays hidden inside encoded text. Push Security reports that four out of five ClickFix attacks it detects reach victims through search engines. That figure comes from the company's own detection data rather than a measurement of all attacks worldwide. Still, it shows why malicious search advertisements deserve attention.

Google confirms it has taken action against the advertiser accounts associated with the reported campaign. "We've suspended the advertiser accounts running the reported campaign. Using ads to distribute malware is an egregious violation of our policies, and we consistently update our detection systems to stay ahead of bad actors' evolving tactics," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy.

Google also says attackers use cloaking to show its advertising review systems different content from what people actually see. The company says it continues monitoring attempts to evade its protections and updating its detection systems.

Microsoft also responded to CyberGuy's request for comment, confirming that its security protections identify the malicious indicators described in the research. A Microsoft spokesperson told CyberGuy, "We take reports of malicious online activity seriously and continuously work to help protect customers from evolving threats. Microsoft Defender protections detect and block the malicious indicators identified in the report." We also reached out to Anthropic for comment on the findings but did not hear back before our deadline.

ANTI-SCAM SETTINGS ON IPHONE, PIXEL AND GALAXY YOU SHOULD CHECK

Scammers are using Google search ads and legitimate Bing redirects to steer Mac users toward a fraudulent Claude AI installer. (Photographer: Daniel Acker/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

You don't need to understand every line of computer code to avoid this scam. A few precautions can help you recognize suspicious downloads before they put your Mac at risk.

Instead of searching for a download and clicking the first sponsored result, go directly to Claude's official download page. Anthropic provides a macOS download there, so you can install the desktop application without relying on an unfamiliar website. You can also access Claude through your browser at claude.ai.

Be especially careful when a website tells you to copy a command into your Mac's Terminal. Terminal commands can download software, change system settings and execute scripts. Even legitimate-looking instructions can become dangerous when they come from an untrusted source. For the regular Claude desktop app, Anthropic provides a downloadable installer. You don't need to paste a command from a search advertisement to get started.

A website's Copy button can place different text on your clipboard than what appears on the page. Before running an unfamiliar command, paste it into a plain-text editor and compare it with the instructions. Watch for unexplained web addresses, encoded strings or commands that download and immediately execute remote scripts. However, even a command that looks harmless may contain hidden risks. When in doubt, stop and verify the instructions with the software developer.

Install macOS security updates and keep your browser current. Additionally, use strong antivirus software that offers real-time protection against malicious downloads and suspicious activity. Security software may help detect harmful scripts or their effects, although no antivirus product can guarantee protection against every attack. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

A sponsored placement means someone paid to promote a link. It does not guarantee that the destination is safe. Before clicking, check the advertiser by selecting the three dots next to a Google search ad. You can review who paid for it and check the advertiser's verification status. Google's Ads Transparency Center at adstransparency.google.com/ offers another way to research advertisers. Always confirm you're visiting the software developer's official website before downloading anything. If an ad looks suspicious, use its three-dot menu to select "Report this ad."

If you pasted an installation command from a suspicious Claude website into Terminal and pressed Return, treat your Mac as potentially compromised. The researchers have not established what the final payload does, so don't assume everything is safe simply because nothing unusual appears on your screen.

WHY VERIFIED SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS CAN STILL LEAD YOU INTO A SCAM

A fake Claude download website displays a legitimate-looking installation command while secretly copying a different command designed to execute a remote script. (Photo Illustration by Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)

What concerns me most about this attack is how much effort the scammers put into making everything look familiar. You start with Google, pass through a legitimate Microsoft service and eventually arrive at a page that looks like it belongs to a popular AI company. Then, with one click of a Copy button, the website quietly substitutes a command that could put your Mac at risk. I've always encouraged people to pay attention to website addresses before downloading software. That's still important, but this case shows why checking the address alone may not be enough. The attackers used trusted services to disguise where their link was taking people. My advice is to go straight to the software developer's official website, especially when installing AI tools. And whenever a download page asks you to run something in Terminal, make sure you understand exactly what you're authorizing. A few extra seconds of caution could save you from a much bigger headache.

Would you trust a software download if it appeared in a Google ad and showed a familiar Microsoft link, or has this kind of scam made you question whether search results can be trusted at all? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Notre Dame faces first real test as unbeaten BYU hosts the Fighting Irish in top-10 clash
excerpt:
Bear Bachmeier connected with Kyler Kasper for a six-yard TD, that gave the BYU Cougars a 21-17 lead against the Arizona Wildcats.

Rankings in college sports can be a bit misleading. It really is har...
body_text:
Bear Bachmeier connected with Kyler Kasper for a six-yard TD, that gave the BYU Cougars a 21-17 lead against the Arizona Wildcats.

Rankings in college sports can be a bit misleading. It really is hard to say who has the best team. One week you can be great; the next, you can suffer. Everyone is relying on people who will go do almost anything other than play professionally.

Teams carry over 50 players, and only two or three from most teams will advance to the professional ranks. Maybe more at some of the best schools. Tonight, we have the #2 team in the country taking on the #8. Do either deserve their ranking?

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Notre Dame comes into the game with a 6-0 record for the season, but I’ll be the first to tell you that I don’t believe in this team. I know there is plenty of talent on their roster, but they aren’t exactly challenged with their schedule.

Notre Dame Fighting Irish quarterback CJ Carr (13) calls an audible at the line of scrimmage against the Pittsburgh Panthers during the fourth quarter at Acrisure Stadium on Nov. 15, 2025. (Charles LeClaire/Imagn Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Beating up on teams that will combine to have a losing record isn’t exactly a major accomplishment. Are CJ Carr’s 1,378 passing yards and 16 touchdowns as impressive as, say, Julian Sayin’s 1,772 yards and 17 touchdowns? Sayin has at least faced Iowa and Texas this season.

This season, the Fighting Irish have played Wisconsin, Rice, Michigan State, Purdue, North Carolina and Stanford. That combination of teams isn’t the worst in football by any means, but they also aren’t ranked teams.

They do have three teams coming up on their schedule who are ranked – today against BYU, Nov. 7 against Miami and Nov. 21 against SMU. They haven’t really had a challenge this season, and only one game could be considered remotely close with an 11-point victory.

BYU quarterback Bear Bachmeier (47) throws a pass during the second half of an NCAA college football game against Cincinnati, Saturday, Nov. 22, 2025, in Cincinnati. (AP Photo/Carolyn Kaster)

WHO'S REALLY PLAYED THE BEST THUS FAR THROUGH THE FIRST HALF OF THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON?

BYU is coming into this game as the top team in the Big 12 and has a perfect record. They are the 8th-ranked team in the country and a loss here, unless very close, will almost certainly drop them down in the national rankings. So far this season, the Cougars have taken down Utah Tech, Arizona, Colorado State, TCU, and Iowa State. I’d argue that they have had a tougher schedule than what Notre Dame has faced.

This team is built around a balance of passing and rushing, instead of being solely focused on one of those games.

Bear Bachmeier, the quarterback, is completing over 65% of his passes for 1,033 yards and eight touchdowns. He has also pulled the ball down and run with it 36 times, second most on the team, and scored four touchdowns. Take him out of the game, and the team has three guys with over 20 carries, averaging over five yards per carry and seven touchdowns. I do wonder if the team will have any success against Notre Dame if they don’t get the ground game going to open the passing attack. Perhaps they will need to get the passing game going to open the running.

BYU quarterback Bear Bachmeier (47) eyes Cincinnati safety Christian Harrison (5) as he runs with the ball during the first half of an NCAA college football game Saturday, Nov. 22, 2025, in Cincinnati (AP Photo/Carolyn Kaster)

The books seem to expect this to be a bit of a defensive battle. The total opened at 54.5, but it has been bet down to 46.5 points. The spread also started at 11.5 in favor of the Fighting Irish. I personally like BYU at home to make this a game. I think their defense can combat some of Notre Dame’s running game. I also think Bachmeier will make this a dynamic game for him. Give me BYU +10.5.

title: Isabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonym
excerpt:
Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits

The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, o...
body_text:
Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits

The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.

Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday with La hora antes del alba, which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired by Chile.

The new story follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.

Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.

“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”

She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.

“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.

Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional title Los que faltan.

However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”

The prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded to La bestia, a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Mola was in fact three male writers – Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.

The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.

Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.

Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”

The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.

title: ‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off
excerpt:
School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments

On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart...
body_text:
School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments

On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.

But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town.

The local comprehensive, King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC), has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field – and it is likely houses will be built on it.

School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.

“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.

“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”

Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealing almost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.

Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”

Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign group Friends of Lower Field, said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”

Lewis Winks, a leading member of the Right to Roam group, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known for progressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate, about a century ago.

A key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.

Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”

The Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”

But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to them are unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.

Matthew Shanks, chief executive of Education South West, said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.

He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.

School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.

Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for six years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.

“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”

title: Inside the long, bitter fight over one man’s quest to build the biggest AI datacenter in California
excerpt:
A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistance

Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, loo...
body_text:
A modern-day prospector promised rural Imperial thousands of jobs and millions in tax revenue – but his plan has set off a firestorm of resistance

Sebastian Rucci zoomed in on a map in late 2024, looking closely at a large block of brown earth. The barren plot sandwiched between sprawling alfalfa fields and sleepy desert suburbs was exactly what he’d been searching for – the perfect place to realize his dream of building the largest artificial intelligence datacenter in California.

The dusty expanse wasn’t an obvious location. It was in the Sonoran desert, just north of the Mexican border, where temperatures regularly rose past 100F (37.8C). Water was scarce in the once-booming agricultural area, which gets its supply from the beleaguered Colorado River. And then, there was the city of Imperial – population 22,000 – to win over. As controversial datacenter projects have sprung up across the US, residents were naturally skeptical of a new, energy-guzzling neighbor.

But for Rucci, a 66-year-old lawyer with a complicated past, none of these obstacles seemed insurmountable.

Rucci is among the new class of middlemen who inhabit the burgeoning world of datacenter development. The rapid rise of artificial intelligence – galvanized by Silicon Valley companies worth trillions of dollars – has fueled one of the biggest industrial construction booms in history. The technology requires far more computing power than traditional internet services, and that means building enormous new structures to house millions of servers.

This proliferation of datacenters is now attracting modern-day prospectors seeking land in hopes of cashing in on one of the fastest-growing and most lucrative industries on Earth. Set in their sights are areas like Imperial county: rural, underdeveloped and desperate for an economic boost.

“I didn’t know much about datacenters,” Rucci said, recalling a couple of years back. “I made calls to people I knew in Silicon Valley. And within a short period, I realized: holy shit, this stuff is huge.”

Rucci, a self-described expert at doing the tedious legwork of packaging permits and plans, proved adept at selling a bright future of economic development to county lawmakers. He said his sales skills also nabbed him a direct line to Google, which floated interest in being the tenant of the datacenter, according to emails between Rucci and county agencies.

With the promise of these potential partnerships and support from construction unions, Rucci moved into high gear last year and began plotting his nearly 1m-square-foot datacenter – a facility the size of 16 football fields combined. He said he had invested about $5m already, and, if it gets approved and passed off to a builder, he expects “big multipliers of that” in return.

What Rucci didn’t expect, however, was the firestorm of resistance his project set off in the community.

Over the past year, more than half a dozen lawsuits have been filed, along with recall efforts for local officials who supported the project. Even a temporary 45-day datacenter moratorium was approved. Echoing similar battles against such development across the US, Imperial county residents told the Guardian they fear increased emissions, harm to the region’s rare desert wildlife, constraints on the power grid and rapidly dwindling water supply, along with noise issues. Rucci denies the project will have such effects.

It seems the backlash succeeded – for now. Rucci’s developments are on pause after a county judge ruled last month that his project cannot move forward until it clears an extensive environmental review. Despite a bold start, Rucci could end up a cautionary tale of what can go wrong when a businessman moves too fast without community buy-in.

“This project was presented as a Noah’s Ark that’s going to come save everybody,” said Francisco Leal, who lives in a residential neighborhood across the street from Rucci’s proposed datacenter. “But the community sees this project as a Trojan horse.”

When Rucci landed on that vast plot of land in Imperial county in late 2024, only two things really mattered: finding a location that could be exempted from California’s strict environmental building requirements, and getting his hands on a lot of electricity. In unincorporated Imperial county, he had both.

Because the land was zoned for industrial use, he was able to apply for an exemption from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), which would fast-track the project by avoiding the environmental permitting process. And for electricity, Rucci was able to work with the local energy provider to eventually get 330 megawatts of electricity – enough to power a city the size of Tallahassee.

Rucci is based in Huntington Beach, but has started several businesses throughout southern California, St Louis and Ohio. In early 2025, he said one of his connections introduced him to a longtime Google employee who helped guide him through the process. In a July email to Imperial county’s planning and development services, Rucci wrote that the datacenter would “enable Google to conduct artificial intelligence and large language model training for its Gemini system”, Google’s suite of AI models.

“We have secured interest from Google for this project, which we are confident will transform the area through increased tax revenues, new employment opportunities, and expanded energy production,” Rucci wrote in another email in August to the county’s air pollution control district.

“We are not involved in a datacenter project in Imperial county,” said a Google spokesperson. She did not respond to questions about the company’s relationship with Rucci. He said Google’s response made sense considering they do not have a formal agreement.

While California has dozens of datacenters capable of cloud computing, streaming and internet searches, the state has scant facilities dedicated to AI. That’s because California is one of the most rigorous states when it comes to environmental permitting for energy and water-intensive facilities such as AI datacenters.

Major projects in California take an average of seven years to get completed, said Michael Thomas, the founder of Cleanview, which tracks datacenter development. For comparison, the average in Texas is about three years. Thomas said he had seen a surge of new players, like Rucci, get into AI datacenter development nationwide. These people, he said, were willing to take on the risk and find ways to speed up the process.

“Land and power have become so scarce at the scale that these big tech companies need,” Thomas said. So, if a developer can shorten the timeline, “a company like Google or Microsoft or Meta may be willing to pay you a huge premium … It’s potentially a way to make millions of dollars very quickly.”

Rucci is no stranger to taking on risk. He has owned a strip club, addiction treatment centers and dozens of accounting and real estate endeavors. In 2010, while operating the strip club, Go Go Cabaret, he was convicted on four counts of illegal liquor sales for which he had to serve a 30-day jail sentence. He was also charged with engaging in a pattern of corrupt activity, money laundering and promoting prostitution, but those charges were later dismissed. In 2019, California suspended his license to practice law for nearly three years.

He has also filed for corporate bankruptcy at least twice. The most recent time, in 2023, took place after the Department of Justice investigated one of his addiction treatment centers for alleged fraud, ending with a government seizure of $600,000 of assets. No criminal charges were filed, however, and that money was later returned with interest after Rucci sued the government to reclaim the seized funds.

Since zeroing in on Imperial county in 2024, Rucci has registered several new businesses related to the vast datacenter campus, from construction and energy supply to ongoing operations. The umbrella company for his project is an LLC called Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing (IVCM). Rucci says the facility will bring in more than 1,600 construction jobs and nearly $30m in annual tax revenue. It will also include an electrical substation, on-site battery energy storage and more than 130 methane-gas-fueled generators, according to an application submitted to the county planning department.

Rucci said his diverse experience was well-suited for such a complicated project. “That doesn’t mean that my background isn’t colorful,” he said. “I’ve challenged cities. I fought the federal government. I’ve done a lot of stuff. But that doesn’t mean that I don’t know how to process this and get it through.”

At first, Leal had no clue that the dusty 75 acres of land across the street from his house had been bought by a developer. It wasn’t until the day before Thanksgiving last year when he found a colorful flyer hanging from his door that his world began to swirl around him. The flyer mapped out the huge project and warned that construction was moving forward without requiring the state’s usual environmental review.

Leal began scanning the internet, and what he found shocked him. His back fence was all that separated his home from Rucci’s property. While Leal lived in Imperial city, the datacenter would fall just outside city limits on unincorporated county land. It was clear that living next to this facility would permanently change the quiet life he and his wife had envisioned when they moved there some 20 years earlier.

“When we bought that house, we planned for it to be the house where we would retire, where our kids would grow up and return when they visit,” Leal said. “The quality of life of anybody living half a mile from the datacenter will be affected.”

He started texting his neighbors that same day. As word spread, people began to organize, holding meetings and rallies against the datacenter proposal. Within months, close to 3,500 people would sign a petition opposing the facility, and state senator Steve Padilla, who represents the district, would sound the alarm, introducing a series of bills aimed at datacenters.

As AI datacenters have popped up around the world, they’ve come under scrutiny for being extremely resource-intensive. A query through chatbots such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Google’s Gemini needs nearly 10 times as much electricity as a typical internet search, and that number can increase for more complicated prompts. Because supercomputers run hot, they typically need extensive water-cooling systems.

Imperial county is a critical habitat for wildlife like the desert pupfish, which is listed as an endangered species under the California Endangered Species Act and swims through agricultural drains and canals, much like one that crosses Rucci’s property. Other desert animals of concern include the flat-tailed horned lizard, yellow-breasted chat and burrowing owls.

As Leal got more involved in the datacenter fight, he met other concerned residents, like Christopher Scurries. Scurries lives nearby and is a music teacher at Imperial high school. He said he was worried about datacenter noise, what’s known as a constant low hum. “I’ll definitely hear when I’m here in my house,” he said. Scurries and his wife moved to the area in 2017 so they could afford a home. Now with a two-year-old daughter, his previously pleasant life feels uncertain in the shadow of the datacenter.

It’s testament to a long-simmering sentiment in this corner of the Sonoran desert, where pollutants from agriculture and industry, along with poverty, have long taken an undue toll. One in five adults is unemployed in the region and the poverty rate, at close to 20%, is the highest in California.

“The benefits these structures may bring into a community – the jobs, tax revenue, even the infrastructure improvements – may feel uncertain or uneven compared to the scale of the impact,” said Carla Walker, the US director of environmental justice and equity at the research organization World Resources Institute. “Communities are asking these questions of who benefits and who pays the price.”

For Jacob Rodriguez, who was born and raised in the area, who pays the price has been top of mind. “It’s an existential threat,” he said of the datacenter project, noting that residents had long dealt with pollution and dwindling water supplies. “The respiratory problems and the air quality here are already abysmal … eventually, indirectly, this will cost lives.”

By March, tensions between Rucci and the community had reached a boiling point. At an Imperial county board of supervisors meeting, dozens of residents, including Leal and Scurries, packed into the chambers for a public feedback session. As Rucci stood at the lectern, trying to present his more than 100 slides on the project, the crowd steadily chanted “no datacenters” and waved “not in my backyard” signs. It got so raucous that Rucci, the main speaker on the schedule, left the meeting early.

As he walked out of the building, protesters yelled “Fuera, Rucci, fuera” (“leave” in Spanish). Visibly fed up, Rucci unexpectedly approached a person screaming through a bullhorn and roared in their face.

By this point, the project was at the center of a heated legal battle. The city of Imperial had sued the county for bypassing public input and environmental reviews when it approved the datacenter (the environmental nonprofit Sierra Club later joined on). Rucci, in turn, counter-sued in federal court on behalf of his company IVCM, alleging the city carried out a “bad-faith campaign of administrative obstruction and targeted retaliation”.

He then went on to sue an anti-datacenter activist named Jake Tison, the Comité Cívico del Valle non-profit, and its executive director, Luis Olmedo, and the local public-media news station KPBS and one of its reporters, Kori Suzuki, for defamation. Those three defamation suits were dismissed. Rucci has appealed in the cases against KPBS and Comité Cívico del Valle and is working to reverse the ruling on Tison.

“Look, I’m not here to run for Miss America or Mr America,” Rucci said. “I’m here to do a datacenter.”

Rucci, on behalf of IVCM, also sued the local utility, the Imperial irrigation district, for rejecting an application for water to cool the datacenter. The utility’s sole source of water is the drought-stricken Colorado River. The AI facility would need about 750,000 gallons of water a day, according to Rucci.

He says the water the datacenter would use is equivalent to a 160-acre farm, of which there are several in the area. The utility’s officials, however, voiced concerns about how the project would affect residents. Karin Euenio, one of the utility’s directors, wrote in an op-ed: “I believe it is my duty to speak up when a proposal raises serious concerns about ratepayers, reliability, and community wellbeing.”

The tumult continued through the spring and summer, with Rucci’s IVCM spending $30,000 in a campaign to back his company spokesperson, Carlos Duran, to fill the seat of one of the utility district’s directors. He lost.

For its part, the community instigated its own political organizing efforts with a recall campaign of Peggy Price, the chair of Imperial county’s board of supervisors who has been supportive of the datacenter. That campaign is ongoing.

While things had been looking good for Rucci after he got county approval for the project in April, it took a drastic turn over the last month. The judge presiding over the city’s lawsuit ruled Rucci must go back to square one for the entire approval process. That means before breaking ground, the datacenter must clear lengthy environmental reviews to assess its impact on the power grid, water supply and emissions.

Alene Taber, a lawyer representing Imperial, said these reviews could take a year or more and that alternative locations for the datacenter would have to be taken into consideration. She said it was meaningful “that there [will be] a transparent, public, environmental process”.

Rucci, however, said he was not deterred and is going to challenge the judge’s ruling. “It’ll be just a matter of time,” he said. “I’m not going away.”

title: Our kids aren’t broken. We need to stop treating every struggle like a disorder
excerpt:
We mobilize all these supports to protect our kids' mental health, but we might actually be working against it. (iStock)

My patient Zach was an objectively awesome tenth grader. He was academically t...
body_text:
We mobilize all these supports to protect our kids' mental health, but we might actually be working against it. (iStock)

My patient Zach was an objectively awesome tenth grader. He was academically talented and motivated, with a mix of A's and A-minuses in accelerated classes. He was a starter on the varsity basketball team. He did Math Olympiad. He even played the French horn in the school band, though he admitted that was mostly for his college application and to get out of an art history requirement that had a reputation for being pretty onerous.

He started preparing for the ACT in April of his sophomore year, hoping to get it over with the following fall. His tutor charged $800 an hour, with a minimum of two-hour sessions, twice a week. Within weeks, he was in my office complaining that there was no way he was going to do well. He couldn't get the pacing right and never finished all the questions in the allowed time. Mind you, he was consistently getting 34s on his practice tests. A perfect score on the ACT is 36. It's an exceptionally rare score. And Zach was very close to it. But Zach wanted to go to the University of Pennsylvania, and he said that a 34 still wasn't good enough. Zach was already in the top percentile of test takers nationally, and he still felt like a failure.

I am a clinical neuropsychologist. I offer psychotherapy and cognitive remediation to children with learning disorders and related developmental disorders. Zach came to see me because he wanted me to write him a letter saying he needed testing accommodations. Maybe with time-and-a-half he’d get the perfect score he really needed.

STUDENTS DIVIDED OVER UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN HIDING FIRST-SEMESTER GRADES FOR 2027 FRESHMEN

When nothing is enough, when excellence is the minimum acceptable, we fall short. And when we fall short, we reach for labels and accommodations and services to close the gap. Of course, sometimes children have real disorders and disabilities, and labels and supports are crucial. But in other cases, the struggles are healthy, normal parts of development, and medicalizing them backfires. The supposed quick fixes may seem helpful in the moment, but more often than not, they make kids even more miserable.

We bring in interventions and services to fix the problem, thinking, 'What's the harm? It can't hurt.' But there's an opportunity cost to everything. (istock)

Zach isn't alone in his anxiety about scores and percentiles. We're all socialized to care about measurements, and we think about how our data compare to everyone else's. From day one, pediatricians measure our kids' height, weight, and even head circumference, and tell us where those numbers fall relative to same-age peers. I remember my son's first checkup. I was so excited to hear that my chunky little guy was in the 95th percentile for both height and weight.

When nothing is enough, when excellence is the minimum acceptable, we fall short. And when we fall short, we reach for labels and accommodations and services to close the gap.

It’s only a matter of time before our obsession with toddler head circumference turns into an obsession with teenage ACT scores. We get emotionally attached to these numbers. We give them more importance than they deserve, and we read them more negatively than we should. I talk to parents all the time who are worried about a score in the 37th percentile. In reality, the 37th percentile is solidly average.

What I usually explain to parents is that in most domains, more isn't better. The average range is wide, and it's the middle that’s often optimal.

Take attention. With too little, we have trouble in school. With too much, we become hypervigilant about tiny, insignificant details and lose the forest for the trees. Anxiety works the same way. Too much and you can't leave the house; too little and you're reckless, walking into oncoming traffic. We want to land somewhere near the healthy middle.

UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN PLANS TO SHIELD 2027 FRESHMAN LETTER GRADES FROM TRANSCRIPTS IN NEW MENTAL HEALTH PLAN

Most scores are also imperfect descriptors of what we can do. We try hard to measure and quantify our traits and abilities, but those measurements are snapshots in time. How we do in a given domain today isn’t necessarily a good predictor of how we'll do tomorrow, since we’re constantly learning, developing, and growing. Also, there's always measurement error. Scores are estimates, not absolutes. And, finally, the best predictors of success are things like perseverance, creativity, and people skills, which usually can't be measured at all.

Katie S. Davis, PsyD., is a clinical neuropsychologist who provides psychotherapy and cognitive remediation to children with learning disorders and related developmental disorders. She is the author of ‘Actually, You’re Fine,’ which was published on Oct. 13, 2026 by Balance, an imprint of Grand Central Publishing. (Balance)

But we're human, and we feel the squeeze from both ends. If our kids are struggling, we see a disorder, and like Zach, we look for a diagnosis and accommodations. If our kids excel, we worry they're perfectionistic, people-pleasing or anxious. We can't win. The messy middle, where most healthy development actually happens, seems to have disappeared.

And this tendency to pathologize everything is making our kids miserable.

GAVIN NEWSOM AVOIDS QUESTION ON BRINGING BACK SAT SCORES AFTER UC OPEN LETTER, ASKS 'SHOW ME THE DATA'

We bring in interventions and services to fix the problem, thinking, "What's the harm? It can't hurt." But there's an opportunity cost to everything. Every minute and every dollar spent on some kind of therapy is a minute and a dollar not spent on soccer practice, day camp, playdates, or regular old homework. The choice isn't between an intervention and doing nothing. It's between an intervention and doing something else with that time and money, something that might bring our kid joy and enrichment (and might even build the perseverance, creativity, and people skills I mentioned earlier).

Of course, we want the best for our kids. I'm not saying we're hurting them on purpose. We get swept up in the same pressure they do. And how could we not? (Getty Images)

We mobilize all these supports to protect our kids' mental health, but we might actually be working against it.

Start with depression. Depression is characterized by helplessness and an external locus of control, the feeling that we aren't in charge of our own destinies. Diagnostic labels locate problems in the brain, outside of kids' control. And when outcomes seem to hinge on rankings and status and paid accommodations, effort stops feeling like it matters.

We need to reframe ‘average’ as good and talk about rankings differently. We need to broaden what counts as success.

Anxiety is similar. Anxiety is maintained by avoidance, and the best treatment involves exposure to the feared thing. When we provide an accommodation that lets our kid avoid whatever seems hard, it brings short-term relief. But we deprive them of the opportunity to learn how to cope. They don’t internalize the message that they can do hard things, and the anxiety grows. We accommodate to relieve the pressure, but the accommodation actually keeps the stress going.

I WORRY LESS ABOUT SCREENS THAN ABOUT THE CHALLENGES TODAY’S TEENS NEVER FACE

Of course, we want the best for our kids. I'm not saying we're hurting them on purpose. We get swept up in the same pressure they do. And how could we not? There's so much mom guilt. We're constantly told that every little decision we make on our kids' behalf matters, and we're trying to navigate an impossible landscape, bombarded with conflicting information. It's hard to separate what's valuable from what isn't, especially with a robust influencer economy that literally profits from our feelings of inadequacy. In that context, a diagnosis makes sense. It partly absolves us, and it offers a clear fix.

If the diagnosis isn't the solution, what is?

We need to reframe "average" as good and talk about rankings differently. We need to broaden what counts as success. We can actively work against helplessness by giving kids real control and crediting their effort and hard work. We can reduce their anxiety by supporting them through hard things instead of constantly removing obstacles. And we have to be honest with ourselves about the difference between support and enabling.

We can actively work against helplessness by giving kids real control and crediting their effort and hard work.  (dusanpetkovic/iStock/Getty Images Plus)

Most important, we should trust our instincts. When there's a real problem, it's usually obvious. In that case, seek help. When there isn't, take a deep breath. Support your kid informally. The struggle will pass, and most likely, it will be a blip on the radar, eventually not mattering nearly as much as we think.

Zach will probably get into a really good college whether he gets a 34 or a 33 or a 35. And he'll probably be a happy, successful human regardless of where he goes to college.

Development is resilient. Let's be resilient, too.

Author's note: The character in this opinion article is a composite and/or fictionalized.

Katie S. Davis, PsyD., is a clinical neuropsychologist who provides psychotherapy and cognitive remediation to children with learning disorders and related developmental disorders. She is the author of the new book "Actually, You’re Fine" published by Balance on Oct. 13, 2026.

title: Ilhan Omar should be jailed, deported if citizenship fraud proven, Top House Republican says
excerpt:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., spoke with Fox News Digital about the federal probe into Rep. Ilhan Omar and what he says should happen if it finds she lied to get citizenship.

EXCLUSIVE: The...
body_text:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., spoke with Fox News Digital about the federal probe into Rep. Ilhan Omar and what he says should happen if it finds she lied to get citizenship.

EXCLUSIVE: The highest-ranking House lawmaker from Rep. Ilhan Omar's home state is calling for the embattled progressive to be jailed and deported if it is found that she or her father lied on federal paperwork to get her U.S. citizenship.

Omar, D-Minn., is under federal investigation over allegations that she or her father lied about her birth year on immigration paperwork in order to obtain her citizenship when her family fled Somalia in the late 1990s. She and other Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., have denounced the probe as political persecution of one of President Donald Trump's detractors weeks before a critical election.

But Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., the No. 3 leader in the House of Representatives, told Fox News Digital that "there have been rumors for years" about Omar and, if proven true, she should face consequences.

"I would say first she should probably serve time in the gray bar motel and then get the hell out of here. She should go back to where she came from" if the allegations are proven to be true, Emmer said. "If it's determined that she lied to gain citizenship, then absolutely, she should go back to the front of the line."

REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES

House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., called for Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., to face consequences if the federal probe into her immigration proves wrongdoing. Omar has criticized the probe as political. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Omar is a member of the House "Squad," a far-left clique that includes Reps. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.

FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION

Federal agents raided Omar's Washington, D.C., home earlier this week and took her cellphone and other possessions.

The allegations stem from her father becoming a U.S. citizen in 2000. Omar was believed to be 17 at the time, and as a minor was automatically qualified for citizenship under U.S. law along with him.

HOMAN CONFIRMS 'CRIMINAL' INVESTIGATION INVOLVING ILHAN OMAR, SAYS HE KNOWS 'THINGS ARE GOING ON’

But recently, it’s been alleged that she was actually 18 and would have needed to go through the process herself at that point.

Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning. (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)

"I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," Omar posted on X after the raid. "I will not be silenced."

DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’

Omar’s allies and other critics of the probe have called it an unprecedented action with less than three weeks before Election Day on Nov. 3.

Jeffries and his top deputies said in a joint statement that the raid was "deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries."

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., is seeking another term in Minnesota’s heavily Democratic 5th Congressional District. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call Inc. via Getty Images)

Emmer argued it was not political. He said that the existence of a judicially authorized search warrant, which the Department of Justice (DOJ) said was being acted on, meant there was a reasonable basis to believe the allegations could be true.

"That judge had to determine that there was probable cause that a federal crime has been committed. And I'll tell you what, as long as it was Ilhan Omar, it was going to be scrutinized to the very detail," Emmer said. "So the fact that they issued the warrant in the first place and then executed it, I mean maybe after all these years, someone is finally going to hold Ilhan Omar accountable."

Fox News Digital reached out to Omar’s congressional office for comment.

Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Leonardo DiCaprio's 'dad bod' puts spotlight on dangerous belly fat — and how to lose it
excerpt:

Rece...
body_text:
Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it.

Recent beach photos of actor Leonardo DiCaprio have reignited the "dad bod" debate — and raised questions about whether carrying a little extra weight around the middle can pose hidden health risks.

The popular term generally describes a softer physique with extra weight around the midsection.

While appearance alone isn’t an indicator of health, excess abdominal fat — particularly visceral fat surrounding the organs — has been linked to an increased risk of heart disease, diabetes and other medical conditions, according to Cleveland Clinic.

YOUR WAISTLINE COULD REVEAL A HIDDEN HEART RISK YOUR BMI MISSES, MAJOR STUDY FINDS

Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it.

Suazo, who has not trained DiCaprio, defines a dad bod as a "loss of structure," an increase in waist circumference and a loss of muscle mass.

Leonardo DiCaprio, 51, soaks up the Hawaiian sunshine as he enjoys a beach day at the luxurious Four Seasons Resort Lanai. The photos have reignited the "dad bod" debate. (BACKGRID)

"Maybe you're losing structure in your day-to-day eating … moving a lot less, taking fewer steps per day," he said of potential causes.

"And typically you're eating and drinking more than you're moving. And the body just starts showcasing that stuff."

BEST FOODS FOR REDUCING DANGEROUS BELLY FAT AND PROTECTING HEART HEALTH

An expanding waistline can be an important indicator of health risk.

According to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, men with a waist circumference greater than 40 inches have a higher risk of developing health problems, including type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

Marfred Suazo, a New York City-based personal trainer known as Fonz the Trainer, spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with excess abdominal fat and ways to reduce it. (Fox News Digital)

Visceral fat — which lies deep within the abdomen and surrounds internal organs — has also been linked to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease, Cleveland Clinic states.

"We want to try to mitigate these things as best as possible before they become an issue," Suazo said.

Reversing a "dad bod" starts with getting nutrition in check, according to Suazo.

That includes understanding daily calorie intake and getting an appropriate balance of protein, carbohydrates and fats.

He recommends pairing that strategy with full-body strength training two to three times per week, focusing on compound movements such as squats, stiff-leg deadlifts, back rows, push-ups and chest presses.

Also among his favorite exercises are pull-ups. "It’s a tremendous exercise that targets the stomach, the biceps and the back," he said, noting that working larger muscle groups can help build overall strength.

An expanding waistline can be an important indicator of health risk, experts say. (Getty Images)

Suazo also recommends incorporating cardio into a well-rounded routine that includes nutrition, strength training and cardiovascular exercise.

Federal physical activity guidelines recommend that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity each week, along with muscle-strengthening exercise on at least two days.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The trainer noted, however, that exercising the abdominal muscles alone won't eliminate belly fat.

"When it comes to belly fat and any fat on the body, we can target our exercises through isolated movements … but we can only reveal it through a loss of body fat throughout the whole body," he said.

"When it comes to belly fat and any fat on the body, we can target our exercises through isolated movements … but we can only reveal it through a loss of body fat throughout the whole body," the trainer said. (BACKGRID)

Suazo said people who improve their nutrition may begin noticing changes within several weeks, although results can vary based on factors including diet, activity level and starting body composition.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Upon four weeks of dialing in your nutrition, you will see a tremendous change in the body," he said.

Nutritional improvements can also boost energy and confidence, the trainer noted, which may help people become more consistent in the gym.

Better nutrition can also support sleep and exercise recovery, he said.

Combining those dietary changes with a smart exercise routine and cardio can create a "recipe for success," according to Suazo.
